A History of Cybersecurity

People, networks, and the cost of trust.

A high-level introduction · Updated October 11, 2026 · University at Albany

Photo: Niklas König / Unsplash

History of Cybersecurity · Part A01 / 40

Teaching aim: explain why cybersecurity evolved as computers became shared, connected, and essential to everyday life. This is a selective history, not a complete list of attacks. No programming background is required. Suggested pacing: 60–75 minutes with discussion. Cover photograph shows vintage equipment photographed recently, not a specific historical incident.

Photo: Niklas König / Unsplash. https://unsplash.com/photos/1cTFuvI14J4. Unsplash License. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

Opening question

A day without digital trust

Imagine that tomorrow you cannot trust one of these. Which failure would affect you first?

Then discuss

What actually goes wrong in each case?

A login failure blocks coursework. A changed balance undermines trust in every later number. A scheduling outage delays care. Cybersecurity protects people who depend on digital systems — it is a social and organizational problem as well as a technical one.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A02 / 40

Interactive: One click per raised hand (right-click undoes). Ask one student per option to explain the consequence.

Ask students to choose one example and explain the consequence. A login problem may block coursework, a changed balance may undermine trust, and a scheduling outage may delay care. Introduce cybersecurity as a social and organizational issue as well as a technical one. These are hypothetical examples.

Foundations

The three familiar security goals

Confidentiality
Only authorized people can read your health record.
Integrity
Your grades stay accurate and changes are traceable.
Availability
You can reach a service when you need it.

A single incident can damage more than one goal.

Which goal is damaged first?

A stranger reads a patient’s recordConfidentiality: information reached someone without authorization.
A grade is changed and no log shows who did itIntegrity: an unauthorized, untraceable change.
Registration crashes on the morning it opensAvailability: the service is unreachable when needed.
A copied exam answer key spreads before the testConfidentiality — and arguably the exam’s integrity too.
Ransomware locks the hospital’s files and leaks some of themAll three can fail at once: files unreachable (A), data leaked (C), trust in the data damaged (I).
History of Cybersecurity · Part A03 / 40

Interactive: Students call C, I or A before you click. The last item is deliberately all three.

Explain the CIA triad in ordinary language. Confidentiality is about access to information, integrity about unauthorized changes, and availability about reliable access. Privacy overlaps with confidentiality but also concerns appropriate collection and use. A ransomware incident may affect all three.

NIST. FIPS 199: Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems (2004). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/final

Before the Internet

Security before networked computers

Physical access

Organizations protected records with locked rooms, trusted staff, and controlled copies.

A lasting principle

Digital security still depends on who can enter, what they can access, and who checks their work.

Think

What can a locked room not prevent?

An authorized person misusing the records. Locks control who enters; they do not check what insiders do. That gap leads straight to access controls and audit.

Photo: Dr. Marcus Gossler

History of Cybersecurity · Part A04 / 40

Use the library as an analogy for managed access, not as evidence of a specific historical security system. Cryptography and physical protection long predate computers. Ask how a locked room helps, and what it cannot prevent if an authorized person misuses records. This provides a conceptual bridge to access controls.

Photo: Dr. Marcus Gossler. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Graz_University-Library_reading-room.jpg. CC BY-SA 3.0. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

1960s

Shared computers, separate identities

Time-sharing

MIT’s CTSS let multiple people use one computer and keep separate files.

The password problem

Passwords helped distinguish users. Sharing a machine created a need to control access.

Think

Why does a shared computer need identities, even inside a trusted university?

Separate files need separate owners. Without identities you cannot say who may read, change, or delete what — or who did it. Identity is the first building block of every later control.

Photo: Computer History Museum / MIT News

History of Cybersecurity · Part A05 / 40

The photograph shows Fernando Corbató using an MIT mainframe in 1965. CTSS was first demonstrated in 1961 and is widely credited with pioneering computer passwords. Avoid claiming that one date captures every early password system. Ask why a shared computer needs identities even inside a trusted university.

MIT News. Professor Emeritus Fernando Corbató, MIT computing pioneer, dies at 93 (15 July 2019). https://news.mit.edu/2019/mit-professor-emeritus-fernando-corby-corbato-computing-pioneer-dies-0715

Photo: Computer History Museum / MIT News. https://news.mit.edu/2019/mit-professor-emeritus-fernando-corby-corbato-computing-pioneer-dies-0715. Historical photograph reproduced for educational commentary. Copyright retained by the rights holder.. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

1960s–1970s

Networking changed the boundary

A shared machine

Access centers on a computer and its local users.

Connected machines

A weakness can reach other people across a network.

Connectivity expands both usefulness and exposure.

Conceptual sketch, not a map of ARPANET

History of Cybersecurity · Part A06 / 40

Interactive: Toggle between the two pictures and ask where the boundary of “our system” now sits.

This is a conceptual comparison of computing arrangements, not a claim that early networks had no security. ARPANET and later Internet systems connected research organizations. Authentication, software flaws, and trust relationships became issues across organizational boundaries.

Leiner et al., Internet Society. A Brief History of the Internet. https://www.internetsociety.org/internet/history-internet/brief-history-internet/

1970s

Security principles that endured

Least privilege

Give each person or program only the access it needs.

Safe defaults

Start restricted; grant permission deliberately.

Separation

Keep one failure from exposing everything.

Usability

Make secure behavior understandable and practical.

Least privilege, live: should a student account get this?

Submit your own assignmentNeeded for the task.
See classmates’ gradesNot needed — and a confidentiality failure.
Read your own gradesNeeded, and only for your own record.
Approve payrollNot needed. Instructors should not get it automatically either.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A07 / 40

Interactive: Ask the room before each click. Then ask what an instructor account should and should not get.

Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 paper described influential principles for protecting computer systems. These slide labels paraphrase selected ideas rather than reproduce the full list. Use a university account: students can submit their work, instructors can grade, and neither should automatically administer payroll.

Saltzer, J. H., and Schroeder, M. D. The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975). https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/protection/

1976

Public-key cryptography

Secure communication without sharing one secret in advance.

Toy key exchange with tiny numbers · public: p = 23, g = 5

Alice sends:
Alice computes key:
Bob sends:
Bob computes key:

Real systems use numbers hundreds of digits long, so an eavesdropper cannot work backward from what is public. This made secure communication easier to scale.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A08 / 40

Interactive: Move either secret: both sides always reach the same key, and the key itself is never sent. Diffie–Hellman with toy numbers; do not present it as how every system works.

Diffie and Hellman published New Directions in Cryptography in 1976, with important related contributions by Ralph Merkle. At a high level, public-key techniques address key distribution and support authentication. Different techniques serve different functions. Do not present the mailbox analogy as a literal explanation of the mathematics.

Computer History Museum. Whitfield Diffie, Fellow profile. https://computerhistory.org/profile/whitfield-diffie/

1977

Encryption becomes a standard

DES
A common encryption method for organizations.
Adoption
Shared standards helped products work together.
Scrutiny
Public analysis tested the design.
Replacement
Growing computing power made it inadequate.

Time to try every key

Bar length on a log scale · illustrative speeds

Cryptographic protection has a lifetime. Each extra bit doubles the work.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A09 / 40

Interactive: Drag the speed up: 56 bits falls within reach; 128 bits does not. DES is a milestone, not current advice.

NBS, the predecessor of NIST, published DES as a federal standard in 1977. Explain that cryptographic protection has a lifetime. DES is a historical milestone, not advice for current encryption. NIST selected AES in 2000 and published the AES standard in 2001.

NIST. Cybersecurity history: Cryptography. https://csrc.nist.gov/nist-cyber-history/cryptography/chapter

NIST. FIPS 197: Advanced Encryption Standard, original publication 2001, updated 2023. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/197/final

1980s

Personal computers widened the problem

Software traveled with people.

Step 1

A shared disk

A friend lends you a disk with a game on it.

Step 2

You run it

The program works — and quietly does something else.

Step 3

It copies itself

Your other programs and disks now carry it.

Step 4

You share again

The next person runs it too.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A10 / 40

Explain the physical movement of software before ubiquitous networking. A virus attaches to or modifies other software and can spread when people run or share it. Avoid naming an absolute first virus because definitions and platforms differ. Ask whether a shared removable drive can still matter today.

NIST. SP 800-83 Rev. 1: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops (2013). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/83/r1/final

1988

The Morris worm

Event
A self-spreading program disrupted computers across the early Internet.
Mechanism
It exploited weaknesses and consumed computing resources.
Consequence
Universities and research organizations struggled to stay available.
Lesson
A connected system can magnify a small program’s impact.
FBI estimate
~6,000

connected computers affected — an estimate, not a precise count

Discuss

Does it matter that the author said he did not intend the damage?

Intent matters for blame and law — Morris became the first person convicted under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. But the consequences were the same whatever the intent. Keep the two questions separate.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A11 / 40

On November 2, 1988, Robert Tappan Morris released the worm. The FBI estimates about 6,000 connected computers were affected. Counts are estimates, so the slide focuses on the well-established disruption. Morris later became the first person convicted under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Keep intent separate from consequences.

FBI. Morris Worm, historical case account. https://www.fbi.gov/history/cases-and-criminals/morris-worm

1988 and after

Incident response becomes a profession

CERT/CC

After the Morris worm, DARPA asked Carnegie Mellon’s Software Engineering Institute to set up a response team.

Coordination

Effective response needs shared information and people who know their responsibilities.

Think

The same vulnerable software runs in many places. Who has to cooperate?

The researcher who found it, the vendor who must fix it, the administrators who must apply the fix, and a coordinator trusted by all of them.

Photo: Frederick Shaw / Unsplash

History of Cybersecurity · Part A12 / 40

The CERT Coordination Center began in 1988. Its role included coordinating vulnerability information between researchers and vendors. The photograph is an illustrative team, not the original CERT staff. Ask which organizations need to cooperate when the same vulnerable software appears in many places.

Carnegie Mellon Software Engineering Institute. Fostering Growth in Professional Cyber Incident Management. https://insights.sei.cmu.edu/history-of-innovation/fostering-growth-in-professional-cyber-incident-management/

Photo: Frederick Shaw / Unsplash. https://unsplash.com/photos/5sdk41pV7yM. Unsplash License. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

Vocabulary check

Virus, worm, and Trojan

Virus
Spreads by attaching to or changing other software.
Worm
Copies itself and spreads between systems.
Trojan
Looks useful or legitimate while hiding harmful behavior.

These labels describe behavior and can overlap.

A free “PDF converter” that also steals saved passwordsTrojan: it looks useful and hides its purpose.
A program that scans the network and copies itself to every vulnerable machineWorm: it spreads between systems on its own.
Code that inserts itself into other programs and runs when they doVirus: it rides on other software.
A game download that secretly opens a back doorTrojan: a legitimate-looking wrapper around harmful behavior.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A13 / 40

Interactive: A quick quiz: class calls each one before you click.

Use this as a brief quiz. A file that pretends to be a useful application fits the Trojan idea. A program that propagates over a network fits a worm. A single malware family can combine characteristics, so categories are explanatory tools rather than perfectly separate boxes.

NIST. SP 800-83 Rev. 1: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops (2013). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/83/r1/final

1990s

The public web raises the stakes

More users

Computing reaches households and businesses.

More services

Shopping and banking move online.

More data

Sites collect personal and payment information.

More trust

People must decide which sites and messages deserve it.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A14 / 40

Interactive: Click through the decade; the next five slides take these one at a time.

The World Wide Web emerged at CERN, with the first proposal in 1989 and important public releases in the early 1990s. Distinguish the web from the older Internet: the web is one service that uses the network. Commercial adoption broadened the stakes of security.

CERN. A short history of the Web. https://home.cern/science/computing/the-birth-of-the-web/short-history-web/

1990s

Firewalls and the perimeter

The perimeter idea

Check traffic as it enters or leaves a network.

The limit

Allowed traffic and trusted users can still cause harm.

A firewall is one layer of protection.

What would a typical perimeter firewall do?

A visitor opens the public course websiteAllowed — the site is meant to be public.
Someone on the Internet tries to log in to the payroll serverBlocked — that service should not face the Internet.
An email with a harmful attachment from an allowed mail serverAllowed. The traffic looks normal; the harm is in the content. This is the limit.
An employee copies records they should not, from insideAllowed — the firewall never sees it. Insiders are past the gate.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A15 / 40

Interactive: The point lands on items 3 and 4: the firewall does its job and harm still gets through.

Use a building entrance analogy. A guard can check entrances but cannot guarantee that every person inside behaves safely. Firewalls apply rules to network traffic, with different types inspecting different information. The analogy is intentionally simplified. Later slides show why identity and internal segmentation also matter.

NIST. SP 800-41 Rev. 1: Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy (2009). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/41/r1/final

1991

Encryption reaches individual users

Pretty Good Privacy

Phil Zimmermann released PGP to help people protect messages and files.

A policy debate

Strong encryption raised questions about personal privacy, public safety, and government access.

Keep it open

Who benefits, and who pays, when private communication is available to everyone?

Journalists, patients, businesses and ordinary users gain privacy; investigators can lose access to evidence. The same property protects both — which is why the debate has never fully closed.

Photo: Benjamin le Roux / Unsplash

History of Cybersecurity · Part A16 / 40

PGP, introduced in 1991, combined established cryptographic techniques in software that individuals could use. The Computer History Museum provides historical context. Keep the policy question open: what benefits and costs arise when private communication becomes broadly available? The notebook is illustrative.

Computer History Museum. Timeline of Computer History: 1991. https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/1991/

Photo: Benjamin le Roux / Unsplash. https://unsplash.com/photos/ePTRLbMD2yQ. Unsplash License. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

1990s

A protected connection on the web

SSL
Helped establish the pattern.
TLS
Became an Internet standard (TLS 1.0, 1999).
What it does
Reduces eavesdropping and helps the browser authenticate the server.

An encrypted connection does not prove a website is honest.

Quick check · the padlock is showing. What does it tell you?

History of Cybersecurity · Part A17 / 40

TLS 1.0 appeared in RFC 2246 in January 1999 and built on SSL 3.0. Modern services use later TLS versions. An attacker can also operate a site with a valid encrypted connection. This distinction helps students avoid treating a browser security indicator as a guarantee of the entire site.

Dierks, T., and Allen, C. RFC 2246: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999). https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2246

Discussion · pairs, 2 minutes

The convincing message

FromDr. Rivera <rivera.office.mail@freemail.example>Sent2:14 a.m.SubjectURGENT — please open before class

Hi all, please review the attached reading before class. I’m in meetings all day, so don’t reply — just open it.

📎 Course_Reading.pdf → opens a sign-in page at docs-share-login.example.net

Click anything that would make you stop and check. Fictional message.
Then

What if it came from Dr. Rivera’s real, compromised account?

Then the address checks out — and every content warning still applies. Trust in the sender and trust in the content are different checks. Confirm through a channel you already trust, and report it.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A18 / 40

Interactive: Pairs find the warning signs first; then click them. There are five.

Allow two minutes in pairs. Strong answers include context, unexpected urgency, the destination, and independent confirmation. A familiar display name is weak evidence. A compromised account can send harmful content. Emphasize usable reporting paths and protective systems rather than blaming people. This is a fictional scenario.

CISA. Secure Our World: Recognize and Report Phishing. https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/recognize-and-report-phishing

1999

Melissa turns email into a delivery system

Entry

An attachment

A malicious document arrives by email.

Spread

Automatic mail

Opening it could send messages to contacts.

Disruption

Mail overload

Email systems faced huge volumes of traffic.

Lesson

Trust as transport

Familiar names help malicious content travel.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A19 / 40

The FBI dates the Melissa outbreak to March 1999. It combined a malicious macro document with automated email distribution. Keep the explanation at the mechanism level. The lesson is about software settings, attachments, and social trust working together.

FBI. The Melissa Virus (25 March 2019). https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/melissa-virus-20th-anniversary-032519

2000s

Cybercrime becomes an organized business

Stolen accounts

Stolen accounts

Say what it means, then click.

Credentials become reusable, tradable assets.

Botnets

Botnets

Say what it means, then click.

Criminals control groups of compromised computers.

Fraud

Fraud

Say what it means, then click.

Stolen access supports theft, spam and impersonation.

Defense

Defense

Say what it means, then click.

Organizations need monitoring as well as prevention.

Discuss

Why does stolen access turn into a market?

Because access is reusable. One group steals passwords, another rents out botnets, another cashes out. Specialization made crime scale — the FBI’s Gameover Zeus case is one example. Defense had to add monitoring, not just walls.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A20 / 40

A botnet is a collection of compromised devices under someone else’s control. The FBI’s Gameover Zeus case illustrates an organized ecosystem of credential theft and related ransomware. This slide describes a broad trend rather than assigning one founding date to cybercrime.

FBI. GameOver Zeus Botnet Disrupted (2 June 2014). https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/gameover-zeus-botnet-disrupted

2003

Slammer spreads at network speed

Weakness
Vulnerable database software on connected computers.
Speed
Most vulnerable hosts infected within about ten minutes.
Harm
Traffic disrupted unrelated services.
Lesson
A patch existed. Delay became a shared problem.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A21 / 40

Interactive: Run at 20% patched, then reset at 80% patched. Patched hosts also protect their unpatched neighbors by not passing it on. A simulation, not Slammer’s real numbers.

CAIDA researchers analyzed the Sapphire/Slammer worm released on January 25, 2003. Their analysis found most vulnerable hosts were infected within ten minutes. The associated weakness had a patch before the outbreak. Keep the scale qualitative on the slide to avoid turning a historical estimate into false precision.

Moore et al. The Spread of the Sapphire/Slammer Worm, CAIDA (2003). https://www.caida.org/catalog/papers/2003_sapphire2/sapphire/

2010

Digital systems control physical processes

Stuxnet

Stuxnet targeted industrial control systems and showed how malware could affect equipment.

A change in consequences

Cybersecurity became inseparable from reliability and physical safety in connected infrastructure.

Think

Why can’t a rail system just reboot overnight to install an update?

Operational technology runs physical processes. Stopping it has safety and service costs, and some equipment runs for decades. Patching becomes a planned operation, not a click.

Photo: Jason Leung / Unsplash

History of Cybersecurity · Part A22 / 40

Stuxnet was discovered in 2010 and targeted industrial control systems. The train station is an illustrative example of infrastructure dependency, not a Stuxnet target. Explain operational technology as computers that help run physical processes. Safety constraints can make updates and shutdowns more complex.

ICS-CERT. Incident Response Summary Report 2009–2011. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ICS-CERT%20Incident%20Response%20Summary%20Report%20%282009-2011%29_S508C.pdf

Photo: Jason Leung / Unsplash. https://unsplash.com/photos/Dd1T5szMbdw. https://unsplash.com/license. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

2013

The Target breach

Access

Through a vendor

Attackers entered through a route linked to a vendor.

Movement

Inside the network

They moved toward systems handling payments.

Warning

Missed chances

A Senate staff report identified chances to interrupt the attack.

Lesson

A chain, not a moment

Vendor access and internal boundaries both matter.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A23 / 40

Use careful attribution: a 2014 Senate staff report analyzed the 2013 Target breach and described apparent missed opportunities. It relied on information available at that time. Avoid presenting every reconstruction detail as settled. The teaching point is that security failures can form a chain.

U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. A Kill Chain Analysis of the 2013 Target Data Breach, majority staff report (2014). https://www.commerce.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/media/doc/2014%200325%20Target%20Kill%20Chain%20Analysis.pdf

2010s

Ransomware turns access into leverage

“Pay to regain access.”

Encrypt
Files become unreadable without a key.
Steal
Copies are taken first, for a second threat.
Threaten
Disruption or public disclosure.
The morning after

Restore and rebuild. Service returns on a plan you practiced. But if data was stolen, backups do not reverse the disclosure.

Bad options only. Rebuild from scratch, or pay with no guarantee the key works — and payment does not prove stolen data was deleted.

Reliable recovery requires preparation before an incident.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A24 / 40

Ransomware predates the 2010s, but it became an increasingly prominent criminal business in this period. Modern extortion may combine encryption and data theft, or use theft alone. Payment does not establish that stolen information has been deleted. Backups help recovery but do not reverse disclosure.

CISA and partners. #StopRansomware Guide (2023). https://www.cisa.gov/stopransomware/ransomware-guide

2017

WannaCry reaches hospitals

May 2017

WannaCry disrupted health services in England and many other organizations worldwide.

The human cost

Unavailable computers can mean delayed appointments, diverted patients, and difficult manual work.

Which security goal failed most visibly?

Photo: Tasha Kostyuk / Unsplash

History of Cybersecurity · Part A25 / 40

The UK National Audit Office investigated WannaCry and the NHS. It found disruption to services and weaknesses in preparedness. The photograph is a general hospital corridor, not an affected NHS facility. Avoid implying that all affected organizations had the same configuration or that one simple fix explains every operational challenge.

UK National Audit Office. Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS (2017). https://www.nao.org.uk/press-releases/investigation-wannacry-cyber-attack-and-the-nhs/

Photo: Tasha Kostyuk / Unsplash. https://unsplash.com/photos/Pk-KuizxQv8. Unsplash License. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

2017

NotPetya and destructive disruption

Your files are encrypted.
Send payment to recover them.
[instructions and an ID code]

Illustrative: it presented itself like ordinary ransomware.

Destructive malware. It caused widespread operational damage far beyond its initial Ukrainian context. Recovery by payment was not a realistic path.

The lesson

The attacker’s message may conceal the actual objective.

Attribution

A 2020 U.S. indictment alleges Russian military involvement — an allegation in a charging document, not a verdict.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A26 / 40

NotPetya spread in June 2017 and harmed organizations far beyond its initial Ukrainian context. The US Department of Justice’s 2020 indictment describes destructive malware and alleged Russian military involvement. Attribution in a charging document is an allegation. Emphasize destructive impact rather than equating it with ordinary recoverable ransomware.

U.S. Department of Justice. Six Russian GRU Officers Charged in Connection with Worldwide Deployment of Destructive Malware and Other Disruptive Actions in Cyberspace (19 October 2020). Charging allegations, not a verdict. https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/six-russian-gru-officers-charged-connection-worldwide-deployment-destructive-malware-and

2017

Equifax exposes a management failure

Known weakness
A software vulnerability required attention.
Follow-through
The patch did not effectively reach the right system.
Sensitive data
Large amounts of personal information were exposed.
Lesson
Responsibility includes verifying the work happened.

When is a patch actually “done”?

A patch notice is not a patch. Avoid reducing the incident to one employee’s error.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A27 / 40

Interactive: Ask which box is the one most organizations skip. GAO points to identification, detection, segmentation and data governance.

GAO’s report describes failures involving identification, detection, segmentation, and data governance. A patch notice alone is not a completed patch. Use this case to discuss organizational accountability and inventory. Avoid reducing the incident to one employee’s error.

U.S. GAO. Data Protection: Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies in Response to the 2017 Breach, GAO-18-559 (2018). https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-18-559

2010s–2020s

Cloud services change the boundary again

Shared infrastructure

Organizations rent computing and storage while relying on providers’ infrastructure.

Shared responsibility

Customers still need appropriate identities, permissions, configuration and data handling.

Photo: Florian Hirzinger

A course folder in a cloud service: whose job?

Locks and guards at the data centerProvider.
Who can open the shared course folderCustomer — the most common place things go wrong.
Replacing failed disksProvider.
Turning on multifactor sign-in for staffCustomer: the provider offers it; you have to use it.
Deciding what data belongs in the folder at allCustomer. A managed service shifts responsibility; it does not erase it.
History of Cybersecurity · Part A28 / 40

The server-room photo is illustrative and does not depict a particular cloud provider. The division of security duties depends on the service, contract, and architecture. A managed service shifts responsibility but does not erase it. Ask who should control permission to a shared course folder.

NIST. SP 800-145: The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/145/final

Photo: Florian Hirzinger. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CERN_Server_03.jpg. CC BY-SA 3.0. Image fitted or cropped for placement.

2020

The SolarWinds supply-chain attack

Trusted path

The supplier

Attackers compromised a software supply chain.

Delivery

A normal update

Some customers received a compromised Orion update.

Follow-on

Selected targets

Some targets faced further intrusion.

Lesson

Verify the chain

A trusted supplier can become part of the attack route.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A29 / 40

CISA issued an alert on December 13, 2020 about exploitation of SolarWinds software. Distinguish receiving a compromised update from suffering every subsequent stage of the campaign. Supply-chain security includes how organizations build, distribute, and verify software.

CISA. Active Exploitation of SolarWinds Software (13 December 2020). https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2020/12/13/active-exploitation-solarwinds-software

2021

Colonial Pipeline links IT to daily life

Incident

Ransomware

It struck the company’s IT systems.

Decision

A proactive halt

The operator stopped pipeline operations on May 7, 2021.

Consequence

Fuel disruption

Deliveries were disrupted until the restart announced on May 13.

Lesson

Dependencies

Business systems and essential services depend on each other.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A30 / 40

The Department of Energy dates the proactive shutdown to May 7, 2021 and the full system restart announcement to May 13. Do not claim that attackers directly controlled the pipeline’s physical equipment. The operational decision itself demonstrates how business IT risk can affect essential services.

U.S. Department of Energy. Colonial Pipeline Cyber Incident (2021). https://www.energy.gov/ceser/colonial-pipeline-cyber-incident

2021

Log4Shell exposes a hidden dependency

One software component. Many affected products.

A serious flaw in the widely used Log4j library created urgent work across organizations in December 2021.

Knowing what your software contains is part of security.

Course portalbuilt in-house
Library searchbuilt in-house
Parking permits appvendor product
Lab instrument softwarevendor product
Email security gatewayvendor product
HR systemvendor product

History of Cybersecurity · Part A31 / 40

Interactive: Search once with the partial inventory (three answers are “ask the vendor”), then switch to a complete inventory and search again. Fictional campus systems.

CISA’s joint advisory explains the Log4j vulnerabilities disclosed in December 2021. A software library is a reusable component that may be embedded in many products. Customers may not know they depend on it. The lesson is inventory, vendor coordination, and timely mitigation rather than exploit mechanics.

CISA and partners. Mitigating Log4Shell and Other Log4j-Related Vulnerabilities, AA21-356A (2021). https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa21-356a

2020s

Zero trust focuses on access decisions

Older assumption

Being inside the network can imply broad trust.

Zero trust

Evaluate each access using identity, context, and policy.

An approach to architecture — not a product, and not distrust of colleagues.

Who
Wants
Device

MFA
History of Cybersecurity · Part A32 / 40

Interactive: Try: student, payroll records, on campus. The perimeter rule allows it; zero trust denies it. Then: payroll staff, payroll records, unusual country. Illustrative policy.

NIST SP 800-207, published in 2020, describes zero trust architecture. It rejects implicit trust based solely on physical or network location or ownership. Zero trust is an approach to architecture, not a single product and not a reason to distrust colleagues as people.

NIST. SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture (2020). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final

2020s

AI changes both sides of cybersecurity

Defenders

AI can help analyze alerts, find weaknesses, and explain complex evidence.

Attackers

The same capabilities can support deception and speed up parts of an attack.

Photo: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Who is using the capability here?

Summarizing thousands of security alerts overnightDefender use.
Writing a fluent scam message in the victim’s own languageAttacker use.
Automatically finding and fixing bugs (DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge, 2025)Defender use — in a competition setting.
Speeding up research on a target organizationAttacker use. The UK NCSC forecasts more efficient intrusion activity through 2027 — a forecast, not a count.

The companion deck, AI & Cybersecurity, develops this.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A33 / 40

The chalkboard research photograph is illustrative. DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge provides a concrete example of automated vulnerability discovery and repair in a competition. NCSC’s 2025 assessment anticipates more efficient intrusion activity through 2027. Clearly identify the latter as a forecast. The companion deck develops this topic.

2024

A major outage can begin without an attacker

The CrowdStrike outage, July 2024

A defective security content update caused widespread Windows system failures. The company stated it was not a cyberattack.

Recovery plans must also account for mistakes in protective tools.

Attacker involved?

The CrowdStrike outage (2024)No attacker — a defective update.
WannaCry (2017)Malicious software.
An administrator accidentally makes a records folder publicNo attacker — but still a security incident: confidentiality failed.
SolarWinds (2020)A deliberate supply-chain compromise.

Security, reliability and safety overlap, but their causes differ. Lessons: staged rollout, recovery capability, knowing your dependencies.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A34 / 40

CrowdStrike’s July 19 statement described a defect in a Windows content update and explicitly said the incident was not a cyberattack. Use this as a category distinction: security, reliability, and safety overlap, but their causes can differ. Lessons include staged deployment, recovery capability, and dependency awareness.

CrowdStrike. To Our Customers and Partners (19 July 2024). First-party incident statement. https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/to-our-customers-and-partners/

2024 and beyond

Preparing for future quantum computers

Future risk
Powerful quantum computers could break some widely used methods.
New standards
NIST finalized its first three post-quantum standards in August 2024.
Long transition
Find and replace vulnerable uses of cryptography.
Present lesson
Plan before a threat fully arrives.

Is your data already at risk? (a planning rule of thumb)

Do not claim present quantum machines can routinely break modern deployed encryption. The third slider is a guess — that is the point.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A35 / 40

Interactive: Blue = migration time, gold = how long the data must stay secret, red line = your guess for the threat. Records stolen today could be read later (“harvest now, decrypt later”).

The standards released in August 2024 cover key establishment and digital signatures. Post-quantum cryptography uses methods designed to resist relevant quantum attacks and can run on conventional computers. Do not claim present quantum machines can routinely break modern deployed encryption.

NIST. Announcing Approval of Three Federal Information Processing Standards for Post-Quantum Cryptography (13 August 2024). https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2024/postquantum-cryptography-fips-approved

Historical synthesis

How the focus expanded

Earlier emphasisAdded as systems connected
Physical accessAccounts and permissions on shared computers
Individual devicesNetworks, suppliers, and shared infrastructure
Keeping attacks outDetection, response, and recovery
Technical controlsGovernance, usable design, and human consequences

Poll · which has changed least?

Earlier protections still matter. New layers accumulate.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A36 / 40

This table is an original synthesis of the history covered. The stages overlap rather than replacing each other. A modern organization still needs physical security and sound access control, even while preparing for AI and quantum-related changes. Ask students which protection they think has changed least.

Practical lessons

A resilient organization

Step 1

Know

Understand important services and their dependencies.

Step 2

Reduce

Limit unnecessary access and maintain systems.

Step 3

Notice

Monitor for problems and make reporting easy.

Step 4

Recover

Practice response and restoration before an emergency.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A37 / 40

Use the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 as a reference for organizing risk management. The slide uses an original teaching summary rather than the official six function names. Explain that resilience involves maintaining or restoring essential service when prevention fails. Governance gives these actions owners and resources.

NIST. Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (2024). https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework

Small-group exercise · 5 minutes

A campus incident tabletop

The course platform becomes unavailable.
A message claims that student records were stolen.

  1. What do you know, and what remains unverified?
  2. Which services need attention first?
  3. Who should communicate with students?
  4. What would make recovery trustworthy?
Group time
Debrief

What did strong groups do?

Kept the theft claim unverified until evidence arrived, preserved evidence, involved the campus response team, used established channels, and planned accessible alternatives for teaching. Map it back to C, I and A.

A useful response separates evidence, decisions, and communication.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A38 / 40

Interactive: Fictional scenario. Reveal one question at a time and start the timer. Do not ask students to investigate live systems.

Fictional scenario. Allow five minutes and assign a spokesperson. Good responses preserve evidence, involve the campus incident response team, use established communication channels, consider accessibility and alternative learning arrangements, and avoid repeating an unverified theft claim as fact. Do not ask students to investigate live systems. Debrief using confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Personal practice

Everyday habits reflect decades of lessons

Account protection

Unique passwords or passkeys, multifactor authentication, and timely updates reduce common risks.

Recovery and reporting

Useful backups and prompt reporting help limit the damage when something goes wrong.

Length beats cleverness — but a reused or leaked password is found instantly, however long. That is why uniqueness and MFA matter.

How big is the search space?

Characters
Attacker

Illustrative: 10 guesses/s online, 1010/s offline. Real attackers try likely passwords first.

History of Cybersecurity · Part A39 / 40

Interactive: Start at 8 lowercase letters offline (minutes), then lengthen to 16. Switch to “online” to show why rate limits matter. Do not have students type real passwords.

Use CISA Secure Our World for practical personal guidance. A password manager can help maintain unique passwords. Phishing-resistant multifactor methods offer stronger protection where available. Backups should be recoverable and separated appropriately. Follow university reporting guidance for suspicious account activity. The photo is illustrative.

CISA. Secure Our World. https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
